newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian oil industry cool to Thursday protest.
newsitem.headline: Russian oil industry cool to Thursday protest.

text.p: Russia's oil sector may see a smattering of vocal protests during nationwide action on Thursday, but senior industry officials said on Wednesday that there would be no disruptions to crude oil output or exports.

"Practically nobody from Novorossiisk will take part in the protests tomorrow, and there certainly won't be any actions to affect operations," said Valentin Korzh, chief engineer at Novorossiisk, Russia's Black Sea oil export outlet.

Oleg Yermenchikov, director of the port's oil terminal, which deals with crude oil shipments arriving via pipeline for loading on to vessels, said very few of the port's 4,000 or so workers would protest and that disruptions to loadings were out of the question.
"I can't speak for everybody at the port, and naturally some people will probably protest, but I can tell you categorically that this will have no effect on loadings," he said.
Russia exports about one third of its 6.2 million barrels per day output.
About 20 million protesters, backed by Russia's communist opposition, are expected by union officials to protest against massive backlogs in wages and pensions.

The average salary in the oil sector is about two million roubles a month, over twice the national average of around 870,000 roubles. There are wage arrears in the oil industry, but they are less severe than the average five-month backlog for other industries.
The general director of Russia's Union of Oil Exporters, Anatoly Yushkin, said unpaid workers might protest, but he had no details on any possible actions.

The oil and gas construction trade union in the oil-rich Komi Republic would call a meeting on Thursday to decide whether to show solidarity with nationwide protestors, Interfax news agency quoted union official Nikolai Yakovlev as saying.
He said about 3,000 workers from oil holding company KomiTEK would attend, but that tensions had decreased because overdue salaries were being paid.
Alexei Gorshkov, spokesman for oil major YUKOS, said he had no information indicating that operations at Russia's second largest oil producer would be affected by Thursday's protests.
"We will have some employees who protest, but not many, because we pay salaries regularly," he said.

A spokeswoman for Surgutneftegaz said from the Siberian town of Surgut, where Russia's third-largest oil producer is based, that Surgut workers would not protest. "We're oil workers and we're well-paid," she added.
